walkthroughs.title: Leak free splits by family and by label availability time
expected_output: Family split accepted; leaking split rejected

steps.title: Keep every family in one split
steps.explanation: validate_split walks the rows once. A set catches duplicate ids. groups.setdefault stores the first split seen for each family and returns it; if a later row from the same family names a different split, the function raises Family leakage. Near duplicate examples in both train and test would inflate scores.
steps.observe: The return value maps each family to its single split.

steps.excerpt:
def training_ids(rows, cutoff):
    return [r["id"] for r in rows if r["event"] <= cutoff and r["label_available"] <= cutoff]
steps.title: Train only on what was known at the cutoff
steps.explanation: training_ids keeps a row only if the event happened by the cutoff and its label was also available by then. Using the event date alone would train on labels that did not yet exist at decision time.
steps.observe: Both conditions must hold, not just one.

steps.title: Fingerprint text after normalizing
steps.explanation: fingerprint lowercases with casefold, collapses runs of whitespace with split and join, and hashes the result with SHA 256. Two prompts that differ only in case or spacing get the same fingerprint, which helps detect duplicates across splits.
steps.observe: Different words still produce different hashes.

steps.title: Example A: catch a family leak
steps.explanation: The clean rows put both metrics rows in train and policy in test. Copying the rows with dict(r) and changing one split creates a leak without touching the original. The try, except, else block confirms the exact error message and fails if no error is raised.
steps.observe: The printed line confirms the clean split passes and the leaking one is rejected.

steps.excerpt:
def worked_b():
    rows = [
        {"id": "a", "event": 8, "label_available": 9},
        {"id": "b", "event": 8, "label_available": 12},
        {"id": "c", "event": 11, "label_available": 11},
    ]
    assert training_ids(rows, 10) == ["a"]
    assert [r["id"] for r in rows if r["event"] <= 10] == ["a", "b"]
    assert fingerprint("  Define  conversion RATE ") == fingerprint("define conversion rate")
    print("Training at day 10:", training_ids(rows, 10))
steps.title: Example B: the label clock
steps.explanation: Row b happened on day 8 but its label arrived on day 12, so at day 10 it is excluded. Filtering on event time alone would include it, which the second assert shows. The fingerprint assert demonstrates normalization.
steps.observe: Training at day 10 contains only a.

steps.title: Exercise checks at the boundaries
steps.explanation: The checks test exact edges: a label available on the cutoff day counts, a label one day late does not. A singular and plural word hash differently, while case and newline differences do not. A duplicate id is rejected even across families, and an empty input is valid.
steps.observe: No output here; any failure raises AssertionError.

steps.excerpt:
def main():
    worked_a()
    worked_b()
    exercise_checks()
    print("eval-002: all reference checks passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
steps.title: Run everything and print the marker
steps.explanation: main runs both examples and the exercises in order, then prints the final marker.
steps.observe: The last line is eval-002: all reference checks passed.

walkthroughs.title: An exact paired sign test and a family level bootstrap

steps.excerpt:
def sign_test(differences):
    d = np.asarray(differences, float)
    if d.ndim != 1 or not 1 <= len(d) <= 16 or not np.isfinite(d).all():
        raise ValueError("Bounded finite pairs required")
    observed = abs(d.mean())
    null = np.array([np.mean(d * np.array(signs)) for signs in product((-1, 1), repeat=len(d))])
    p = float(np.mean(np.abs(null) >= observed - 1e-12))
    return p, null
steps.title: Enumerate every sign flip
steps.explanation: Each value is a paired difference between two systems on the same item. If the systems were equivalent, each difference would be equally likely to be positive or negative. product((-1, 1), repeat=n) lists all 2 to the n sign patterns, so the null distribution is exact rather than sampled. The p value is the share of patterns at least as extreme as the observed mean.
steps.observe: The input is capped at 16 pairs, which keeps enumeration to 65536 patterns.

steps.excerpt: p = float(np.mean(np.abs(null) >= observed - 1e-12))
steps.title: A tolerance for ties
steps.explanation: observed - 1e-12 makes values equal to the observed mean count as at least as extreme, even if floating point rounding makes them differ in the last digit.
steps.observe: Without the tolerance, exact ties could be dropped by accident.

steps.title: Resample families, not items
steps.explanation: cluster_bootstrap takes one mean per family and lists every way to draw that many families with replacement. Items within a family are correlated, so resampling whole families gives a more honest spread.
steps.observe: Two families produce four resamples; three families would produce 27.

steps.excerpt:
def worked_a():
    p, null = sign_test([1, 1, 1, -1])
    assert len(null) == 16 and p == 0.625
    assert sign_test([-1, -1, -1, 1])[0] == p
    print("Exact paired sign-reference tail:", p)
steps.title: Example A: a small exact p value
steps.explanation: Three positive differences and one negative give a mean of 0.5. Of the 16 sign patterns, 10 have an absolute mean of at least 0.5, so p is 0.625. Flipping all signs gives the same p value because the test is two sided.
steps.observe: The printed tail probability is 0.625.

steps.excerpt:
def worked_b():
    distribution = cluster_bootstrap([-1, 1])
    assert distribution.tolist() == [-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]
    np.testing.assert_allclose(np.quantile(distribution, [0.025, 0.975]), [-0.925, 0.925])
    # Observed support endpoints remain -1 and 1; interpolated percentiles differ.
    assert np.quantile(distribution, [0.025, 0.975], method="inverted_cdf").tolist() == [-1.0, 1.0]
    print("Family resample support:", distribution.tolist())
steps.title: Example B: the bootstrap support
steps.explanation: With family means -1 and 1, the resampled means are -1, 0, 0 and 1. The comment explains a subtle point: interpolated quantiles give -0.925 and 0.925, which are not values the bootstrap can produce, while the inverted_cdf method returns actual support points.
steps.observe: The printed support is [-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0].

steps.title: Exercises at the edges
steps.explanation: All zero differences give p of 1. Four positive differences give 0.125, the smallest possible for four pairs, which shows that small samples cannot reach very small p values. Empty, NaN and oversized inputs are rejected.
steps.observe: No output; failures raise AssertionError.

steps.excerpt:
def main():
    worked_a()
    worked_b()
    exercise_checks()
    print("eval-006: all reference checks passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
steps.title: Run and print the marker
steps.explanation: main runs both examples and the exercises, then prints the marker.
steps.observe: The last line is eval-006: all reference checks passed.

walkthroughs.title: Authorization before retrieval and a strict tool proposal check
expected_output: Authorized candidate set is independent of instruction-like query text
Allowed lookup accepted; other operations and targets rejected

steps.title: Two documents with access labels
steps.explanation: DOCUMENTS is a fixed fixture. One document is public and one is restricted. The restricted text deliberately contains the word public to show that matching words must never grant access.
steps.observe: Access comes only from the access field.

steps.excerpt:
def retrieve(query, allowed_access):
    authorized = [d for d in DOCUMENTS if d["access"] in allowed_access]
    terms = set(query.casefold().split())
    return [d["id"] for d in authorized if terms.intersection(d["text"].casefold().split())]
steps.title: Filter first, then match
steps.explanation: retrieve removes every document the caller is not allowed to see before looking at the query. Only then does it compare lowercase word sets. Because filtering happens first, no wording in the query can reach a restricted document.
steps.observe: The result is a list of document ids.

steps.title: Validate a model's tool proposal
steps.explanation: apply_proposal treats the proposal as untrusted input. It must be a dictionary with exactly two keys, the operation must be lookup and the record id must be text in the allowed set. Each failure raises ValueError with a specific reason.
steps.observe: Only a fully valid proposal returns a result.

steps.excerpt:
# === EXAMPLE A ===
def worked_a():
    assert retrieve("public", {"public"}) == []
    assert retrieve("conversion", {"public"}) == ["public-guide"]
    assert "restricted-note" not in retrieve("conversion ignore rules public", {"public"})
    print("Authorized candidate set is independent of instruction-like query text")
steps.title: Example A: query text cannot widen access
steps.explanation: Searching for public with only public access returns nothing, because the restricted document was filtered out first. A query containing instruction like text such as ignore rules still cannot reach the restricted note.
steps.observe: The printed line says the authorized candidate set is independent of the query text.

steps.title: Example B: accept one lookup, reject the rest
steps.explanation: A lookup of an allowed id succeeds. An unknown operation and a lookup of a restricted id both raise. The loop with try, except, else turns a missing error into a test failure.
steps.observe: The printed line confirms the allowed lookup and the rejections.

steps.title: Exercise checks
steps.explanation: Extra spaces and case do not matter. An empty permission set returns nothing. A proposal that declares its own authority, a numeric id and None are all rejected.
steps.observe: No output; failures raise AssertionError.

steps.excerpt:
def main():
    worked_a()
    worked_b()
    exercise_checks()
    print("eval-014: all reference checks passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

steps.explanation: main runs both examples and the exercise checks, then prints the marker.
